title: What happens when security tools go dark before the ransomware
content_md: On Oct. 1, threat researchers reported that the China-linked group behind Warlock ransomware, which Microsoft tracks as Storm-2603, had attacked at least four organizations in the prior two months. A water utility and a telecommunications provider were among them, along with a regional government body and a university. This all occurred in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries across Europe, Africa and Latin America. The likely way in was on-premises Microsoft SharePoint. The researchers believe the group still carries the ToolShell flaws it exploited in July 2025, the same month Microsoft shipped the fixes, alongside newer SharePoint flaws. An exploit for a bug patched more than a year ago is still worth packing. Somewhere, a server is still waiting for its fix. Before I ran a security company, I ran its finances. The habit I kept is reading the assumption under every number. Equipment is expected to keep producing. Inventory is expected to sell. When the assumption breaks, the asset gets written down. Security budgets carry one too, and almost nobody writes it down. It is that the tools on the books will still be running when the attack arrives. Warlock’s operators went after that assumption directly. Nine days in, 2 hours to disarm One intrusion, against a critical infrastructure operator, shows the pattern.
